options: A Display implementation
A Debug implementation that prints the type's name and fields
An equality implementation
A default constructor
quiz.explain: It generates a Debug impl usable with {:?}, printing the type's name and every field's value.

options: It doesn't — they're unrelated traits
Copy is defined as `trait Copy: Clone`, so any Copy type is also a Clone type
Clone requires Copy, not the other way around
It's a historical accident with no real reason
quiz.explain: Copy is bounded by Clone (`Copy: Clone`) — a Copy type is always also Clone, since copying is the cheap, implicit version of cloning.

quiz.q: Why can't a struct with a `String` field derive `Copy`?
options: Strings are too large for Copy
String owns heap data and can't be safely duplicated by copying bits; it only implements Clone, not Copy
Copy only works on enums
You need to derive PartialEq first
quiz.explain: Copy requires every field to itself be Copy. String owns a heap allocation and only implements Clone, so a struct containing it can't derive Copy.

options: Floats are too imprecise for any comparison
NaN != NaN breaks the reflexivity Eq/Ord require, so floats only implement PartialEq/PartialOrd
f64 doesn't support == at all
Eq only works on integer types
quiz.explain: Eq promises full reflexivity (a == a is always true), which NaN violates; floats implement PartialEq/PartialOrd but not the stricter Eq/Ord.

quiz.q: What determines the sort order for a struct with `#[derive(PartialOrd, Ord)]`?
options: Alphabetical order of the field names
The order the fields are declared in the struct, most significant first
The field types' sizes in bytes
It's random unless you specify a key
quiz.explain: Derived ordering compares fields in declaration order, exactly like comparing a tuple — the first field is the most significant.

quiz.q: What happens if you `#[derive(Debug)]` on a struct where one field's type doesn't implement Debug?
options: That field is skipped in the output
The whole struct fails to compile
It prints "?" for that field
It falls back to Display for that field
quiz.explain: Deriving requires every field to implement the trait; one field missing Debug fails the entire derive at compile time, not just that field.

quiz.q: What does `..Default::default()` do in a struct literal?
options: Copies every field from a previous instance of the same value
Fills in any fields you didn't explicitly set with their type's Default value
Only works if the struct implements Copy first
Only applies to tuple structs
quiz.explain: It's struct update syntax combined with Default — you set the fields you care about, and the rest fall back to Default::default() for their types.

quiz.q: When should you hand-write a trait instead of deriving it?
options: Never — always derive when possible
When the mechanical field-by-field behavior isn't what you actually want, e.g. custom equality that ignores one field
Hand-writing is always required for Debug specifically
Only for enums, never structs
quiz.explain: Deriving gives you the mechanical field-by-field version; hand-write when semantics should differ, like case-insensitive equality or ordering by a subset of fields.

quiz.q: What does `HashMap`/`HashSet` require of its key type?
options: Only Debug
Both Eq and Hash
Only PartialOrd
Only Clone
quiz.explain: Keys need Eq (so equal keys are recognized as the same key) and Hash (so equal keys land in the same bucket).

flashcards.back: An implementation of the Debug trait, enabling {:?} printing of the type's name and fields.

flashcards.front: Clone vs Copy — what's the practical difference?
flashcards.back: Clone is an explicit .clone() call (deep copy); Copy makes assignment implicitly duplicate the value instead of moving it.

flashcards.front: What must be true of every field for a struct to derive Copy?
flashcards.back: Every field must itself implement Copy — no String, Vec, Box, or other heap-owning type.
Because NaN != NaN violates the reflexivity Eq requires; f64 only implements PartialEq.

flashcards.front: What order does derived PartialOrd/Ord compare struct fields in?
flashcards.back: Declaration order, top to bottom — like comparing a tuple, first field most significant.

flashcards.front: What does Hash + Eq together enable?
flashcards.back: Using the type as a key in a HashMap or HashSet.

flashcards.front: What happens when you derive a trait but one field doesn't implement it?
flashcards.back: The whole derive fails to compile — it isn't silently skipped.

flashcards.front: Give one reason to hand-write PartialEq instead of deriving it.
flashcards.back: When equality should ignore some fields (e.g. an internal cache) or use custom logic (e.g. case-insensitive string comparison).
